insider_note: Both radicals are already standard Sin⁻¹ integrals, 1/√(1−x²) and 1/√(1−y²), so separating the variables and integrating each side directly is all that is needed here too.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. Move one radical term to the right side, then divide to isolate dy and dx on opposite sides.
steps.memory_tip: √(1−x²) and √(1−y²) under a square root are the exact building blocks of the two standard Sin⁻¹ integrals.
steps.why: Moving the √(1−y²)dx term to the right and then dividing through by both square roots separates the equation completely, with the y terms and dy on one side and the x terms and dx on the other.
common_mistakes: Losing the minus sign when moving √(1 − y²)dx across to the other side.
Dividing by only one of the two square roots and leaving the other factor mixed in with the wrong variable.

steps.label: Integrate and finish
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Both sides integrate directly to a Sin⁻¹ — no substitution needed.
steps.memory_tip: ∫1/√(1−x²)dx = Sin⁻¹x is another standard integral worth knowing by heart, alongside the Tan⁻¹ one.
steps.why: Both sides are exactly the standard integral form ∫1/√(1−t²)dt = Sin⁻¹t; integrating each side and moving the Sin⁻¹x term across to the left gives the symmetric final relation Sin⁻¹y + Sin⁻¹x = c.
common_mistakes: Writing the integral of 1/√(1−x²) as Tan⁻¹x instead of Sin⁻¹x, confusing the two standard forms.
Leaving the answer as Sin⁻¹y = −Sin⁻¹x + c without combining it into the neater Sin⁻¹y + Sin⁻¹x = c form.
